item.title: One family, two generations and a shared love for aviation for the Singh family
item.description: For more than three decades, the Singh family has shared a journey that has taken them from humble beginnings and personal sacrifice to the skies with Fiji’s national airline. What began with two people finding their way into aviation has grown into a two-generation family story shaped by hard work, sacrifice, family support and a shared love for flying.
item.content:encoded:
For more than three decades, the Singh family has shared a journey that has taken them from humble beginnings and personal sacrifice to the skies with Fiji’s national airline.

What began with two people finding their way into aviation has grown into a two-generation family story shaped by hard work, sacrifice, family support and a shared love for flying.

Together, Sharmila and Satpreet Singh and their two sons, Prashant and Satvikrant, have accumulated close to 90 years of aviation experience across Fiji Air, Air Pacific and Fiji Airways.

For Sharmila, the journey began when she was working at an accounting firm and noticed cabin crew members visiting the office.

She had hoped to become a teacher, but watching the crew come and go sparked her curiosity about aviation and eventually led her towards a career with the airline.

In February 1992, she put on the Air Pacific uniform for the first time as cabin crew and is now a Purser .

Sharmila says wearing the uniform for the first time made her feel proud, nervous, and excited.

As Sharmila and her husband built their careers, their growing family became accustomed to the rhythm of airline life, rosters, early starts, travel and periods of time apart.

For Sharmila, seeing her sons eventually step into the same industry became one of the most meaningful moments of her journey .

She says seeing her sons in uniform is one of the proudest moments of her life.

She says it is more than seeing them dressed as pilots, it is seeing their dreams, hard work, and dedication come to life.

Her husband, Satpreet, the fascination with aviation began when he was a boy growing up in Wailailai, Ba.

Satpreet shares that any time an aircraft was in the sky, he would automatically look up.

He says his parents were teachers at Khalsa College, where the family lived in the teachers’ quarters among the sugarcane fields.

His father and mother had migrated from Punjab, India, to Fiji in the late 1950s and went on to become an important part of the Khalsa College community.

That fascination with aircraft eventually became a dream of becoming a pilot.

His first flight came as a child on a holiday with his mother.

It would be years before he boarded an aircraft again, and when he did, it was as a student pilot.

When Satpreet told his family he wanted to fly, money was tight, but they found ways to support him.

His father gave whatever savings he could, while his mother surrendered her life insurance policy and took out a loan.

His sister also took out a loan to help fund his flying school, while his brother provided accommodation and logistical support in Kilbirnie, Wellington, New Zealand.

Satpreet also worked at the flying school, cleaning and refuelling aircraft, as well as cleaning offices and lavatories.

He also worked at a kitchen and bathroom showroom to help support himself.

For Satpreet, every job was another step towards his dream.

He joined Fiji Air in 1991, flying the DHC6 Twin Otter, BN2A Islander, Harbin Y-12 and Embraer EMB110 from Nausori before joining Air Pacific in 1999 as a Boeing 737 First Officer.

He became a Captain in 2007 and continued his flying career through the evolution of the airline and its fleet .

Thirty-five years into his commercial flying career, Satpreet has logged more than 23,000 flying hours, mostly in jets, and remains driven by the same passion.

Meanwhile, none of the Singh brothers was pressured to follow their parents into aviation.

For Prashant, aviation had simply been part of life for as long as he could remember.

Prashant says he grew up surrounded by aviation because of their parents and their colleagues, so there was always a curiosity and a natural pull towards it.

item.title: Taveuni family travels 10km for water amid concerns over delivery delays
item.description: He says they received water last Wednesday and lodged another request after their supply ran low. The resident says they waited several days before another delivery was made on Sunday after he contacted a senior official for assistance.
item.content:encoded:
He says they received water last Wednesday and lodged another request after their supply ran low.

The resident says they waited several days before another delivery was made on Sunday after he contacted a senior official for assistance.

He says they were expecting another delivery on Wednesday, but the water cart had not arrived at the time he spoke to fijivillage News.

The resident says when there is no water at home, his family has to travel about 10 kilometres to another water source to wash and collect water.

He says they sometimes make the trip at night because the water source is beside the road, making it difficult for the family to bath during the day.

The resident says the situation is also difficult for the children, who have to prepare for school the following morning.

For drinking water, the family is buying bottled water, which the resident says now costs about $21 a carton compared to around $18 previously.

He says his family is only asking for a reliable water delivery service and clearer information on when deliveries will be made.

The resident also alleges that some water cart workers became upset with him after he contacted senior officials when earlier requests were not attended to.

Insert: Resident on water cart delay. 23rd Sep 26

He says he only escalated the matter because his family needed water and they were not getting a clear response on when a delivery would be made.

The resident is calling for water cart requests to be attended to on time as families continue to deal with the water shortage.

fijivillage News is seeking a response from the relevant authorities regarding the concerns raised by the resident.

item.title: Online abuse can push women out of public and political life – Peterson
item.description: Speaking during a panel discussion on technology-facilitated gender-based violence in political life, National Coordinator for the Fijian National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Women and Girls, Laisani Peterson says online abuse can silence women, damage their reputation and create fear about participating in public life. She says violence against women online should not be treated separ
item.content:encoded:
Speaking during a panel discussion on technology-facilitated gender-based violence in political life, National Coordinator for the Fijian National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Women and Girls, Laisani Peterson says online abuse can silence women, damage their reputation and create fear about participating in public life.

She says violence against women online should not be treated separately from violence experienced offline, as both can be linked to gender inequality, power imbalances and harmful social attitudes.

Peterson says women should be able to speak, lead, campaign and participate in public and political life without fear of abuse or retaliation.

She says addressing technology-facilitated gender-based violence should not be left to survivors to address alone.

Peterson says Government, political parties, law enforcement agencies, civil society organisations, communities and online platforms all have a responsibility to respond.

She says political parties should have clear codes of conduct, condemn online abuse and support women candidates and leaders who are targeted.

Peterson says parties should also ensure their members and supporters are not contributing to harassment, misinformation or intimidation.

She says clear reporting processes and support services are needed for survivors, while online platforms should remove harmful content quickly and cooperate with authorities.

Peterson says the Online Safety Commission has also become a signatory to Fiji's revised service delivery protocol, providing another avenue for people to report online harm through its toll-free number 1548.

She says preventing technology-facilitated gender-based violence is not only about online safety, but also about ensuring women and girls can participate in public life safely and confidently.

item.title: Dreaming of medicine since childhood: Brian Malani’s journey to becoming a Doctor
item.description: After watching films as a child, Brian Malani was inspired to pursue his childhood dream of becoming a doctor, driven by the desire to help people in a medical facility. Malani, who hails from Nabukadra in Ra and shares maternal links to Tailevu, completed his secondary school at Marist Brothers High School in 2008.
item.content:encoded:
After watching films as a child, Brian Malani was inspired to pursue his childhood dream of becoming a doctor, driven by the desire to help people in a medical facility.

Malani, who hails from Nabukadra in Ra and shares maternal links to Tailevu, completed his secondary school at Marist Brothers High School in 2008.

At 19 years old, he was later offered a scholarship to study medicine in China.

Malani says he first studied the Chinese language at Tongji University before pursuing medicine at Southeast University.

He says one of the challenges he faced was learning Chinese and Mandarin within a short period of 10 months, which was an uphill battle for him.

Malani recalls attending his first class at the university, where he had hoped to meet other Pacific Islanders and fellow Fijians . However, he was the only Fijian in a class dominated by Chinese students, along with students from other countries.

The RFMF captain says learning basic conversations was critical, and he was fortunate to study alongside other foreign students, which made the transition easier.

He says he kept the students motivated by encouraging them to struggle together.

This inspired the group to learn the language within the 10-month period.

Malani says that after completing the 10 months of language study, the students were separated according to their chosen fields of study, including law, fashion and medicine.

He says his first experience in the classroom was an unforgettable one as he had to find ways to fit into a class where the students did not understand English and spoke only Mandarin.

Despite the language barrier, he tried his best to speak and greet his classmates.

Insert: Malani on first day of class 26th Sep

Malani says he studied medicine for six years in China before graduating and returning to Fiji, where he spent some time at Colonial War Memorial Hospital and worked alongside former Health Minister Dr Iferemi Waqainabete.

He says working at CWM Hospital presented another challenge because he had studied medicine entirely in Chinese.

Hearing medical terms in English meant he had to translate them into Chinese in order to understand them.

Malani says that after two years of internship, he gradually became familiar with the system and found himself back on familiar ground.

He says he joined the Republic of Fiji Military Forces in 2019 and later travelled to Iraq, where he served his duty as a medical doctor for the army.

When asked about his biggest motivation, Malani says his parents, particularly his mother, and his siblings were his greatest source of hope.

They encouraged him to keep praying, regardless of the challenges he faced.

He says he found comfort in talking to his mother.

Malani recalls opening his books and seeing everything written in Chinese.

At times, he would ask himself what he was doing there, but thoughts of his family pus hed him to persevere and complete his studies.

His message to children is to stay away from drugs, continue to trust in the Lord and listen to their parents.

Malani is challenging children across Fiji to pursue their dreams, value education and leave the rest in the hands of the Lord.

item.title: Sewage discharge and strong stench raise concerns along Tomanu Road, Nadera
item.description: A strong sewage stench along Tomanu Road in Nadera is raising concerns for residents, with the Nasinu Town Council confirming that sewage from a burst sewer line has been entering a roadside drain. Nasinu Town Council CEO Felix Magnus says the Council inspected the site on the 14th of last month, after receiving a complaint from a resident.
item.content:encoded:
A strong sewage stench along Tomanu Road in Nadera is raising concerns for residents, with the Nasinu Town Council confirming that sewage from a burst sewer line has been entering a roadside drain.

Nasinu Town Council CEO Felix Magnus says the Council inspected the site on the 14th of last month, after receiving a complaint from a resident.

Magnus confirms that the liquid is sewage.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Nasinu resident Ashwani Kumar says the smell is extremely strong and unpleasant, causing significant discomfort and concern in the area.

Kumar says the purplish-brown liquid appears to be entering the drain from somewhere nearby, rather than coming from the drain itself.

He says the source of the discharge should be investigated to determine whether it poses any health or environmental risks to people living and travelling in the area.

When asked whether the Nasinu Town Council is taking any action on the matter, Magnus says the Council was advised that the Water Authority of Fiji had rectified the sewer line on 13th August, but it burst again.

He says the Council referred the matter to WAF, as the sewer line is an asset of WAF.

He says all sewer-related complaints are referred to WAF.

When questioned, WAF says they will visit the site and reconfirm the situation.
